data.command: How does power shell execution work for attackers?

data.text:
PowerShell execution is ATT&CK T1059.001 — the Windows command interpreter used as a scripting host. For a Linux web box like this the interesting part is how it looks coming off the wire from a compromised web app, so here's the shape of it.

Microsoft ships powershell.exe (Desktop 5.1, System32\WindowsPowerShell\v1.0) and pwsh (Core, cross-platform). Attackers almost never type interactively on a victim; they get the binary invoked for them by a parent process: WINWORD.EXE or EXCEL.EXE via a VBA macro, wscript/cscript via a .js or .vbs, mshta.exe via an .hta, rundll32 or regsvr32, a service or scheduled task, WMIC /node: process call create, WinRM, PsExec, or an Office add-in. Parent-child relationships like winword.exe -> powershell.exe are the highest-fidelity signal available.

Execution styles, roughly in order of how often they show up:
- -EncodedCommand with a Base64 string. PowerShell expects UTF-16LE, so the blob looks like it is stuffed with NUL bytes between printable characters. Combined with -nop -w hidden -noni -ep bypass it is the classic "you can't read my command line" move.
- -Command with the script inline, often semicolon-chained, sometimes with backticks or ^ folding to break naive string matching.
- -File pointing at a dropped .ps1, or a .ps1 staged in %TEMP%, %APPDATA%, ProgramData, or a public folder.
- IEX / Invoke-Expression fed by a download cradle: Net.WebClient, DownloadString, DownloadFile, Invoke-WebRequest, or bitsadmin/certutil to fetch stage two. The cradle is what makes it fileless — nothing touches disk except maybe the AMSI scan buffer.
- Reflective loading: [Reflection.Assembly]::Load() or LoadFrom with a .NET binary, then invoking a method, so the payload never lands as an executable.
- Add-Type compiling C# in memory, or Invoke-Mimikatz / Invoke-Kerberoast style tools built as PS1 modules.
- Runspace and PSEtw / AMSI patching: PSEtwLogProvider, amsiInitFailed, or memset on AmsiScanBuffer to blind the logging pipeline before the real work starts.
- Constrained Language Mode and WDAC/AppLocker bypass attempts, PowerShell v2 downgrade via -version 2 to dodge 5.x logging, and -WindowStyle Hidden with no console.

What lands in logs when it runs: 4688 or Sysmon 1 for process creation with the full command line (only if CommandLine auditing is on), ScriptBlock logging 4104 with the deobfuscated script text, Module logging 4103, PowerShell operational 4103/4104, transcription files, AMSI 1101, and Defender's "PowerShell/..." signatures. Sysmon also catches network egress if the cradle phones home.

On my side of the fence, a web app RCE that pivots to Windows almost always reaches PowerShell over WinRM 5985/5986, SMB 445, or a web-delivered .hta/.js. That is why I keep an eye on 5985/5986 and 445 outbound from the DMZ — a single 10.x connection to a workstation's WinRM port is not something my app ever needs to do.
